q: Why is ordinary linear regression inappropriate for a binary outcome such as relapse (yes/no)?
o: Predictions can fall outside 0–1, and the linearity and normal-error assumptions fail
It cannot include more than one predictor when the outcome variable is coded as 0 and 1 in the data file
It always gives an R² of exactly zero when the outcome has only two possible values
It requires the predictors to be binary as well as the outcome, which is rarely the case
e: A straight line fitted to 0/1 data predicts probabilities below 0 or above 1, the relationship between predictors and probability is S-shaped rather than linear, and errors cannot be normal or homoscedastic. Logistic regression models the log odds instead, which keeps predicted probabilities between 0 and 1.
w: Linear regression can include many predictors whatever the outcome coding.
R² isn't automatically zero for a 0/1 outcome; the problem is invalid predictions and assumptions.
Predictors can be of any type; only the outcome is binary here.
k: Binary outcomes → logistic regression, because linear predictions escape 0–1 and assumptions fail.
h: Straight lines can't bend to fit yes/no.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Why not linear regression

q: Logistic regression is linear in which quantity?
o: The logit, the natural log of the odds of the outcome
The probability of the outcome occurring, from 0 to 1
The odds ratio of the outcome for each predictor
The −2 log-likelihood of the model, step by step
e: ln[P/(1 − P)] = b0 + b1X1 + … The probability itself follows the S-shaped curve P = 1 / (1 + e^−(b0 + b1X1 + …)). Each b is the change in log odds per unit increase in its predictor.
w: Probability follows an S-shaped curve, not a straight line.
Odds ratios are exponentiated coefficients, not the linear quantity.
−2LL measures fit, not the quantity the model is linear in.
k: Logistic regression is linear in the logit, ln(odds).
h: Log the odds, straighten the S.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · The logit

q: A logistic model has b0 = −1 and b1 = 0.5. What is the predicted probability of the outcome when X = 4?
o: About .73
About .50
About .27
About .62
e: Logit = −1 + 0.5 × 4 = 1. P = 1 / (1 + e^−1) = 1 / (1 + 0.368) = .73. At X = 2 the logit would be 0, giving P = .50.
w: .50 is the probability when the logit is 0, which happens at X = 2.
.27 is the probability for a logit of −1, the reverse sign.
.62 uses a logit of 0.5, forgetting the intercept.
k: Compute the logit, then P = 1 ÷ (1 + e^−logit).
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Predicted probabilities

q: A predictor has B = 0.50 in SPSS's 'Variables in the Equation' table. What is Exp(B), and what does it mean?
o: About 1.65: each one-unit increase multiplies the odds of the outcome by 1.65
About 0.50: each one-unit increase raises the probability of the outcome by 0.50
About 1.65: each one-unit increase raises the probability of the outcome by 65 percentage points
About 0.61: each one-unit increase cuts the odds of the outcome by about 39%
e: Exp(B) = e^0.5 = 1.65, the odds ratio: odds are multiplied by 1.65, a 65% increase in odds, per unit increase in the predictor. Odds ratios change odds, not probabilities. The effect on probability depends on where you start on the S-curve.
w: B is a change in log odds, not in probability; Exp(B) is 1.65.
Odds ratios multiply odds; they don't add percentage points to probability.
0.61 is e^−0.5, which flips the sign of B.
k: Exp(B) = odds ratio: odds multiply by Exp(B) per unit increase.
h: Exponentiate B to get the odds multiplier.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Exp(B)

q: An Exp(B) of 0.50 means that a one-unit increase in the predictor:
o: Halves the odds of the outcome
Halves the probability of the outcome
Reduces the probability by 50 percentage points
Has no effect, since Exp(B) is below 1
e: Exp(B) < 1 means the odds decrease: 0.50 means the odds are multiplied by 0.5, a 50% reduction in odds. Exp(B) = 1 means no effect. The 95% CI for Exp(B) should exclude 1 for a significant predictor.
w: Odds ratios change odds, not probabilities.
Exp(B) doesn't subtract percentage points from probability.
Exp(B) below 1 means the odds decrease, which is an effect.
k: Exp(B) < 1 = odds decrease; 1 = no effect; > 1 = odds increase.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Odds ratios below 1

q: −2LL is 154.08 for the constant-only model and 144.16 after adding one predictor. What is the model chi-square?
e: Model χ² = −2LL(baseline) − (−2LL(new)) = 154.08 − 144.16 = 9.92, with df equal to the number of parameters added (1). The predictor significantly improves on the baseline model, which predicts the most common category for everyone. SPSS shows this in the Omnibus Tests of Model Coefficients table.
w: 298.24 adds the two −2LLs instead of subtracting.
One predictor adds one parameter, so df = 1, not 2.
0.06 is roughly R²_L, not the model χ².
k: Model χ² = −2LL(baseline) − −2LL(new), df = parameters added.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · The likelihood ratio test

q: For the same model, what is Hosmer and Lemeshow's R²_L?
o: About .064
About .936
About .002
About .640
e: R²_L = model χ² / −2LL(baseline) = 9.92 / 154.08 = .064, the proportional reduction in badness of fit. Pseudo-R² values are typically much smaller than linear-regression R², and different versions (Cox & Snell, Nagelkerke) give different numbers.
w: .936 is 1 − R²_L, the remaining badness of fit.
.002 is the p-value, not R²_L.
.640 misplaces the decimal; 9.92/154.08 ≈ .064.
k: Hosmer and Lemeshow's R²_L = model χ² ÷ −2LL(baseline).
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Pseudo-R²

q: Why does SPSS report Nagelkerke's R² alongside Cox and Snell's?
o: Cox and Snell's can never reach 1, so Nagelkerke rescales it to a 0–1 range
Cox and Snell's is used for categorical predictors and Nagelkerke's for continuous ones
Nagelkerke's is the only one that tests whether the model is significant
Cox and Snell's measures overdispersion, while Nagelkerke's measures fit
e: Cox and Snell's R² has a maximum below 1 (about .75 for some data), which makes it hard to interpret. Nagelkerke divides it by that maximum, so a perfect model reaches 1. Neither is a proportion of variance explained in the linear-regression sense.
w: Neither R² depends on whether predictors are categorical or continuous.
Model significance comes from the model χ², not Nagelkerke's R².
Neither R² measures overdispersion; both describe fit.
k: Nagelkerke rescales Cox and Snell's R² to reach 1.
h: Nagelkerke stretches Cox and Snell to the top.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Cox and Snell vs Nagelkerke

q: In the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, which result suggests the model fits well?
o: A non-significant result (p > .05)
A significant result (p < .05)
A value of −2LL that is above 100
A Nagelkerke R² above .50
e: The test compares observed with predicted frequencies across groups of predicted risk. A significant result means they differ, indicating poor fit, so non-significance is what you want. Like other fit tests, it is affected by sample size.
w: A significant result means observed and predicted differ: poor fit.
−2LL values don't indicate good fit by size alone.
Nagelkerke's R² isn't the Hosmer–Lemeshow test.
k: A non-significant Hosmer–Lemeshow test indicates the model fits well.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Hosmer–Lemeshow test

q: A predictor has B = 1.20 and SE = 0.40. What is its Wald statistic, and what is a known weakness of the Wald test?
o: Wald = 9.00; with large b its SE inflates, making the test too conservative
Wald = 3.00; it is overly liberal in small samples, causing Type I errors
Wald = 9.00; it cannot be computed when predictors are categorical
Wald = 0.33; it ignores the standard error of the coefficient
e: Wald = (b / SE)² = (1.2 / 0.4)² = 9.00, compared with χ²(1), giving p ≈ .003. When b is large, its SE tends to be inflated, so Wald underestimates significance, raising Type II errors (Menard). The likelihood ratio test, comparing models with and without the predictor, is more reliable.
w: 3.00 is b/SE before squaring, and Wald is conservative, not liberal.
Wald can be computed for categorical predictors.
0.33 divides SE by b, and Wald does use the SE.
k: Wald = (b/SE)²; it's conservative for large b, so prefer likelihood ratio tests.
h: Wald wobbles when b is big.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · The Wald statistic

q: The classification table in SPSS logistic regression output shows:
o: How many cases the model classifies correctly, using a cut-off of .5 by default
The odds ratio for each predictor, together with its confidence interval
The −2LL at each step, showing whether the model is improving as it goes
The categories of each categorical predictor, together with their contrast codes
e: Cases with a predicted probability above the cut value (.5 by default) are classified as 1, and below as 0. Compare overall % correct with Block 0 (the constant-only model) to see whether the predictors improve classification, and look at sensitivity and specificity, not just the overall figure.
w: Odds ratios appear in Variables in the Equation.
−2LL by step appears in the Iteration History and Model Summary.
Categorical coding appears in a separate coding table.
k: Classification table: correct classifications at a .5 cut-off; compare with Block 0.
h: How often did it guess right?
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Classification table

q: How is the assumption of linearity of the logit usually tested?
o: Add each continuous predictor's interaction with its own log; significance means violation
Plot the predicted probabilities against each continuous predictor and check that they form a straight line
Compute VIF values for each predictor and check that all of them are below 10
Run the Hosmer–Lemeshow test separately for each continuous predictor in turn
e: The Box–Tidwell approach adds X × ln(X) for each continuous predictor. If that term is significant, the relationship between X and the logit is not linear. Probabilities are expected to be S-shaped, so a straight-line plot of them is not the right check.
w: Probabilities are expected to be S-shaped, not straight.
VIF checks multicollinearity, not linearity of the logit.
Hosmer–Lemeshow tests overall fit, not linearity per predictor.
k: Test linearity of the logit with X × ln(X) terms (Box–Tidwell).
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Linearity of the logit

q: Complete separation occurs when:
o: A predictor (or combination) perfectly predicts the outcome, so estimates explode
Two of the predictors are perfectly correlated with each other in the sample being analysed
The two outcome categories have exactly equal numbers of cases in the sample
The model includes no constant term, so it cannot be estimated by maximum likelihood
e: If every case above some X value is a 1 and every case below is a 0, the maximum-likelihood b heads toward infinity and its SE becomes huge, often with a warning that estimation stopped. Remedies include more data, combining categories, or penalized (Firth) regression.
w: Perfectly correlated predictors cause multicollinearity, not separation.
Equal numbers in the two outcome categories don't cause separation.
Omitting the constant isn't what complete separation means.
k: Complete separation: a predictor perfectly predicts the outcome, so estimates blow up.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Complete separation

q: In logistic regression, a dispersion parameter well above 1, say above 2, suggests:
o: Overdispersion: variance exceeds what the binomial model expects, so SEs are too small
Underdispersion: the model is too conservative, so the standard errors and CIs are too large
Perfect fit: the model explains all of the variance in the binary outcome
Multicollinearity: two of the predictors explain the same variance in the outcome
e: When the variance exceeds the model's expectation (common with clustered or aggregated data), SEs and CIs are underestimated and significance is overstated. Values near 1 are fine, and above 2 are problematic. The dispersion parameter can be estimated by dividing the deviance (or Pearson) χ² by its df.
w: Values below 1 would indicate underdispersion, not above 2.
A dispersion parameter doesn't indicate perfect fit.
Dispersion concerns outcome variance, not multicollinearity.
k: Dispersion above 2 = overdispersion; SEs are too small.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Overdispersion

q: How can multicollinearity be checked for a logistic regression in SPSS?
o: Run a linear regression with the same predictors and inspect the VIF and tolerance
Tick 'Collinearity diagnostics' in the Binary Logistic dialog's Options box
Inspect the classification table for any cells with zero counts in them
Check whether the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test is significant
e: Collinearity depends only on the predictors, not on the outcome, so the collinearity statistics from linear regression (VIF, tolerance) apply. SPSS's logistic procedure does not provide them directly.
w: The Binary Logistic dialog has no collinearity option.
Zero-count cells relate to separation, not collinearity.
Hosmer–Lemeshow tests model fit, not collinearity.
k: Check logistic collinearity by running a linear regression with the same predictors.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · SPSS · Collinearity in logistic regression

q: In SPSS's Binary Logistic dialog, what does the 'Categorical' button do?
o: Declares categorical predictors and sets their contrast, such as indicator with a reference
Declares that the outcome variable is categorical, which must be done before every logistic analysis
Converts continuous predictors into categories by splitting them at their medians
Sets the cut-off probability value used to build the classification table
e: Predictors listed as categorical are dummy-coded automatically. Indicator contrasts compare each category with a reference category (first or last, which you choose). Without this, a multi-category code would be treated as a continuous number.
w: The outcome is already binary; Categorical concerns predictors.
The Categorical button doesn't median-split continuous predictors.
The cut-off is set under Options.
k: The Categorical button dummy-codes predictors using chosen contrasts.
h: Tell SPSS which predictors are groups.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · SPSS · Categorical predictors

q: If a stepwise method must be used in logistic regression, which is preferred, and why?
o: A likelihood-ratio method (such as Backward: LR), because the Wald statistic is unreliable
A Wald-based method (such as Forward: Wald), because likelihood-ratio tests are the unreliable ones
A conditional method, because it is the only stepwise method that SPSS can run
Enter, because stepwise methods cannot be used at all in logistic regression
e: Stepwise entry is best avoided for theory testing. When it is used for prediction or exploration, selection based on likelihood-ratio tests is more trustworthy than Wald-based selection, given the Wald statistic's inflated SEs.
w: Wald-based methods are the unreliable ones.
SPSS offers several stepwise methods, not only conditional.
Stepwise methods can be used, though cautiously.
k: If stepwise is used in logistic regression, prefer likelihood-ratio methods.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Methods of entry

q: An outcome has three unordered categories (CBT, medication or no treatment chosen). Which analysis is appropriate?
o: Multinomial logistic regression, comparing each category with a reference
Binary logistic regression, using the category codes 1–3 as the outcome
Ordinal regression, ranking the treatments from least to most effective
Linear regression with the treatment choice as the dependent variable
e: Multinomial logistic regression estimates a set of logistic equations, each comparing one category with the reference category (for example CBT vs none and medication vs none). In SPSS: Analyze → Regression → Multinomial Logistic. Ordinal regression would only fit if the categories were ordered.
w: Binary logistic handles only two categories.
Ordinal regression requires ordered categories, which these aren't.
Linear regression can't model unordered categories.
k: Unordered outcome with several categories → multinomial logistic regression.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Multinomial logistic regression

q: Which diagnostics can be saved from SPSS logistic regression to look for influential cases?
o: Cook's distances, leverage values, DFBeta and standardized residuals
VIF, tolerance and Durbin–Watson values for every predictor in the model
Mauchly's W and the Greenhouse–Geisser estimates for each predictor
Box's M and Levene's statistics for each of the predictor variables
e: The Save button offers predicted probabilities, group membership, Cook's, leverage, DFBeta, and standardized, studentized and deviance residuals. Similar thresholds to linear regression apply: about 95% of standardized residuals within ±2, Cook's below 1, and DFBeta below 1.
w: VIF and Durbin–Watson come from linear regression.
Mauchly's W is for repeated measures.
Box's M and Levene's are ANOVA/MANOVA checks.
k: Save Cook's, leverage, DFBeta and residuals to find influential cases.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Diagnostics

q: Which is a well-reported logistic regression result for a predictor?
o: R² = .64, so the model explains 64% of the variance in relapse, with b = 0.50 and p = .003 for the predictor
t(98) = 2.94 for the predictor, p = .003, with R² = .64 for the model as a whole
The predictor raised the probability of relapse by 65%, p = .003, so it is a strong risk factor
e: Report b, its SE, the test (Wald, or preferably LR), p, the odds ratio with its CI, and overall model fit (model χ², Hosmer–Lemeshow and Nagelkerke R²). Avoid describing odds ratios as changes in probability, and do not interpret pseudo-R² as variance explained.
w: Pseudo-R² isn't variance explained, so '64% of the variance' misleads.
Logistic regression uses Wald or LR tests, not t.
Odds ratios change odds, not probability by 65%.
k: Report b, SE, Wald/LR test, p, OR with CI, and model fit.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · Logistic regression · Reporting

q: In SPSS output, Block 0 ('Beginning Block') shows the model with:
o: Only the constant, which predicts the most frequent outcome for everyone
All of the predictors entered at once, before any of them are removed
Only the predictors that were significant in a previous analysis of the same data
The interaction terms only, entered without any of the main effects
e: Block 0 is the baseline: with only an intercept, every case is predicted to belong to the larger outcome category. Its −2LL and classification accuracy are the benchmark against which Block 1 (with the predictors) is compared.
w: All predictors appear in Block 1.
Block 0 doesn't use previous analyses.
Block 0 has no interaction terms.
k: Block 0 = constant only, predicting the most common outcome.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 21 · SPSS · Block 0
